Wiring Listeners into app.js →

Side-Effect Imports and Registration Order

events/index.js registers three listener files by importing them for what they do at load time, not for anything they export.

Each channel from this lesson's diagram — in-app, email, realtime — lives in its own file under src/events/listeners/, and each one calls domainEvents.on(...) for every event it cares about, right at the top level of the module, the moment that file is first imported. Nothing needs to be exported from any of them for that registration to happen — importing the file is the registration. One file pulls all three in purely for that effect:

// Figure 5.6: importing three files for what they do, not what they export (src/events/index.js)
import './listeners/notifyInApp.listener.js';
import './listeners/notifyEmail.listener.js';
import './listeners/notifyRealtime.listener.js';

This is a side-effect import — no { ... }, no default binding, nothing assigned to a variable. Node still has to run the whole module to import it at all, and running it is exactly what calls .on() three or four times inside. Deleting one line here (say, notifyEmail.listener.js) switches email notifications off entirely without touching that listener file, the emitter, or any service — the clearest possible demonstration of Topic 1's whole argument that reacting to an event is decoupled from announcing it.

The order of these three lines only matters in one narrow way: EventEmitter calls listeners for the same event in the order they registered, so if one listener threw synchronously, later ones for that same event wouldn't run. None of the listeners in this lesson rely on that ordering — each wraps its own work in try/catch specifically so one channel's failure can never reach, or block, another (next topic covers why).
